narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 56.3% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were by far the strongest influence. Both placed you at the very bottom of your school’s performance distribution—second decile in year one and first decile in year three—well below the average of accepted students, who typically rank around the sixth decile. These unusually low academic standings strongly pushed the model toward predicting failure.

Your LSAT score of 35.5 and undergraduate GPA of 3.4 worked in the opposite direction. Both are respectable and actually helped pull the prediction back toward passing. However, they were not strong enough to overcome the heavy negative signal from your class rankings.

Your family income, gender, race, and full-time status played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance to the middle of your class in the remaining years. Stronger grades will directly address the factor that most hurt your prediction. Consider retaking the LSAT if you can reach a meaningfully higher score, and then reapply.
